title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation:Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry

paper.title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model’s behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results.
However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation.
We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions.
Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length.
Motivated by the concentration of teacher–student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns.
Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6 % 54.6\% , achieving the best scores of 0.558 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many LLM applications repeatedly answer questions using the same long documents, such as technical manuals, scientific literature, legal texts, or organization-specific knowledge. Placing those documents in the inference context is effective ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , but repeatedly processing them wastes computation and context-window capacity. Context distillation instead injects a fixed document into model parameters: the document-conditioned model teaches the same model without the document, enabling closed-book inference without a stronger teacher, gold labels, or a verifier ( Askell et al., 2021 ; Snell et al., 2022 ; Kujanpää et al., 2025 ) . Recent distillation methods increasingly replace off-policy teacher-generated data with on-policy supervision of the student’s own sequences ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ) ; training on states encountered at inference reduces train–inference mismatch and often improves behavior transfer ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , motivating the same extension to context distillation ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . When context distillation is used for knowledge injection, however, we observe a surprising reversal: across two document-QA datasets, pure on-policy context distillation (OPD) is consistently weaker than off-policy distillation. Prior work separately points to weak reverse-KL supervision outside the student’s effective support ( Minka, 2005 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and inadequate rollout coverage of teacher-preferred behavior ( Lazaridis et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . We ask how these two limitations interact when the teacher’s only advantage is information absent from the student’s input. We study this interaction in a controlled context-distillation testbed whose documents contain random key–code mappings unavailable from the model’s prior knowledge. We vary two properties of the codes independently: token-level unpredictability and length. For each setting, we run the full generation-source × \times KL-direction grid. The results show how properties of the knowledge to be injected control the interaction between the two limitations. Reverse KL fails regardless of generation source, making the objective the primary bottleneck; once forward KL restores the token-level signal, student rollouts become limiting as the codes grow longer. Thus, under the information asymmetry of knowledge injection, OPD is least efficient exactly where the document contributes the most content the student cannot infer on its own. The implication is selective rather than global: OPD should be retained where the teacher–student mismatch is modest, with intervention reserved for positions where document-specific information creates a large coverage gap. We therefore propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), which uses a per-token divergence gate to jointly adapt the rollout and objective. At high-divergence positions, APD shifts sampling toward the teacher and the loss toward forward KL; otherwise, the gate remains nearly closed and training stays effectively on-policy. As the student learns, the divergence falls and both interventions shrink toward OPD. APD requires neither gold answers nor a verifier, yet raises OPD from below every off-policy baseline to parity with the strongest of them on our benchmarks. Our contributions are as follows: • Using a controlled context-distillation testbed, we show how token-level unpredictability and sequence length expose distinct OPD bottlenecks along KL direction and generation source (§ 4 ). • We propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose reversible per-token divergence gate jointly adapts sampling and KL direction without gold answers or a verifier (§ 5 ). • Using real documents, ablations reproduce the testbed’s bottleneck hierarchy and show that intervening at only a small fraction of tokens recovers most of the gain (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: 2.1 Knowledge Injection via Distillation
sections.text: Ye et al. (2026) apply on-policy context distillation to system prompts and solution traces, whereas we study the internalization of document-specific knowledge unavailable in the student’s input. Closest to our setting, GATES distills from document-conditioned tutor traces using consensus gating ( Stein et al., 2026 ) , MixSD combines conditioned and unconditioned predictions at a fixed ratio ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and EDGE-OPD guides student rollouts with a fixed teacher mixture while masking the loss using binary teacher evidence ( Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) . Beyond distillation, document knowledge can also be injected by synthetic continued pretraining ( Yang et al., 2025b ) . These interventions reflect a broader difficulty of on-policy distillation: teacher-preferred content with low student probability is unlikely to be effectively learned. Prior analyses show that student rollouts rarely reach such content ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) , while some methods exclude teacher preferences outside the student’s effective support as unteachable ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . In knowledge injection, however, these low-support tokens are precisely what must be learned. Related work further shows that forward and reverse KL can behave differently under finite training budgets despite sharing the same optimum ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and that prefix source and KL direction can be varied independently ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We extend this analysis to knowledge injection and use a single adaptive, reversible per-token gate to control both prefix generation and the distillation objective, rather than relying on fixed mixtures or hard masks.

sections.heading: 2.2 Bridging the Teacher–Student Mismatch
sections.text: Token-level remedies for teacher–student mismatch fall into three groups. Sampling-side methods replace student tokens outside the teacher’s top- K K (SKD) ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , let the teacher intervene when token probabilities diverge (SWITCH) ( Koo et al., 2025 ) , or switch to teacher generation after a moving divergence threshold (AdaSwitch) ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . Schedule-side methods interpolate an intermediate teacher (TAID) ( Shing et al., 2025 ) or anneal a global forward-to-reverse KL mixture with a coverage-based brake (CADENCE) ( Kumar and Jha, 2026 ) . DistiLLM adaptively schedules student-generated data ( Ko et al., 2024 ) , while DistiLLM-2 pairs different losses with teacher- versus student-generated data ( Ko et al., 2025 ) . Loss-side methods blend KL directions per token via probability-ratio weights on fixed data ( Jung et al., 2025 ) or mask unteachable tokens ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Each intervenes on sampling, scheduling, or loss alone; APD instead uses one state-dependent per-token signal for both the sampling mix and KL direction. sections.heading: 3 Problem Setup
sections.text: We consider a self-distillation problem where the teacher is the frozen base model conditioned on the document, hence any teacher–student difference is purely informational ( Stein et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) . Let d d be a document to internalize and x x a question about it. An autoregressive model defines π ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = ∏ t π ⁡ ( y t ∣ s t ) \pi(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}\pi(y_{t}\mid s_{t}) over responses y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) , where s t = ( x , y < t ) s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) denotes the state at step t t . The teacher is the frozen base model with the document in its context, π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) = π 0 ( ⋅ ∣ d , x , y < t ) \pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})=\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid d,x,y_{<t}) . The student π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) never sees the document and starts from the same base model without it, π 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) \pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) . The goal is for the student to reproduce the teacher’s document-conditioned behavior without reading d d . In the distillation family studied here, the student is trained against the teacher’s full next-token distribution rather than against sampled tokens as hard labels: the loss is a per-token divergence D D between student and teacher, summed over the states of a sampled response ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ) . Writing ρ \rho for the distribution of y y , the family is ℒ ⁡ ( θ ) = 𝔼 y ∼ ρ [ ∑ t D ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) , π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ) ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\theta)={}&\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho}\Big[\sum_{t}D\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big)\Big].\end{split} (1) Recipes within it differ along two axes. The first is where the loss is evaluated : the generation source ρ \rho is either a fixed corpus of teacher-generated responses, independent of the current student, on which the student is teacher-forced ( off-policy ), or the student’s own rollouts, resampled as the student changes ( on-policy ). The second is which divergence is minimized : D D is either the forward KL D KL ( π T ∥ π θ ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{T}\|\pi_{\theta}) or the reverse KL D KL ( π θ ∥ π T ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T}) . Of the four resulting combinations, two are the recipes used in practice. PD (per-token off-policy distillation) applies forward KL on teacher-forced states, i.e. word-level KD ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . OPD applies token-level reverse KL to the document-conditioned teacher on the student’s own rollouts ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . The remaining two, reverse KL on teacher-forced states (off-rev) and forward KL on student rollouts (on-fwd), are rarely used on their own: the two choices travel together in practice ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . One further reference, SFT , falls outside Eq. 1 altogether: it fits sampled teacher tokens as hard targets without consuming the teacher logits.

sections.heading: 4 Why On-Policy Distillation Fails to Inject Knowledge
sections.text: Injection concerns knowledge the student does not have, so measuring it cleanly calls for a target the student genuinely cannot know. We build one synthetically. The context is a key–value store: a fixed document listing N = 64 N{=}64 lines of the form “ The code for {key} is {code}. ” The codes are drawn at random, so the document is the only place they exist and no amount of prior knowledge substitutes for reading it. For each key, we ask the probe “ What is the code for { key } ? Output only the code, nothing else. ” The teacher and student share the same base model, but only the teacher receives the key–value store as document context in its system turn. The resulting asymmetry is therefore purely informational. To answer correctly, the student must internalize the key → \to code mapping in its weights. Closed-book exact-match recall over the N N keys therefore directly measures how many mappings have been successfully injected. To test how the form of the knowledge affects how readily it is internalized, we vary the alphabet size ( | Σ | ∈ { 2 , 10 , 16 , 36 , 62 } |\Sigma|\in\{2,10,16,36,62\} ) and code length ( L ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } L\in\{2,4,8,16,32,64,128\} ). These two variables control how unpredictable each code is and how many tokens must be learned in sequence. We quantify each cell’s difficulty by the mean teacher-forced, closed-book negative log-probability of its gold codes under the base model, − log ⁡ p base ​ ( code ) -\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(\text{code}) . The resulting values range from 21 21 to 632 632 nats. This controlled construction lets us vary target difficulty and length separately, which is not possible with real-data benchmarks. On this grid we run all four cells of § 3 , with SFT as a hard-target reference and all other settings held fixed across cells. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix C.1 .

sections.heading: Where the signal vanishes.
sections.text: OPD minimizes the reverse KL at states the student itself visits: ℒ OPD = 𝔼 y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ ∑ t D KL ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ∥ π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ) ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}={}&\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\\ &\Big[\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big)\Big].\end{split} (2) Equation 2 combines two choices that can bottleneck injection: the reverse-KL objective and the student-generated state distribution. The full generation-source × \times KL-direction grid in Figure 1 separates their effects. We first examine the KL direction. Across the figure, both reverse-KL variants lag behind their forward-KL counterparts regardless of generation source. Even in the easiest top-left cell, both forward-KL runs saturate within 100 100 steps, whereas both reverse-KL runs are still climbing at step 400 400 . To see why, hold the sampled state s s fixed and consider the gradient with respect to the student logit of a token a a : π θ ( a ∣ s ) [ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) π T ​ ( a ∣ s ) − D KL ( π θ ∥ π T ) ] . \begin{split}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\Big[&\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{T}(a\mid s)}\\ &-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{T}\big)\Big].\end{split} (3) The gradient is scaled by π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) \pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) and therefore vanishes as π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) → 0 \pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\to 0 . Reverse KL thus provides little first-order signal for raising a low-probability token, which is its zero-forcing property ( Minka, 2005 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Jung et al., 2025 ) . A derivation and its assumptions are given in Appendix A . Document-specific tokens are precisely the tokens that the student initially considers unlikely and injection must raise. The bottom-left panel makes this dependence visible. At fixed length, a wider alphabet makes each target symbol less probable under the student; as Equation 3 predicts, the resulting reduction in gradient magnitude increasingly prevents both reverse-KL variants from learning the codes. Both forward-KL conditions remain at ceiling, while the near-overlap of the two reverse-KL conditions shows that the generation source makes little difference in this regime. The second bottleneck lies in the student-generated state distribution. On-policy training places the loss on whatever the student generated. But the student has never read the document, so at the positions that carry document-specific content it has nothing to produce the right token from; these are exactly the positions at which its rollouts leave the target. For example, suppose the target code is ABCD , but the student samples X as its first symbol. Every subsequent loss is then evaluated at prefixes beginning with X , rather than at the target prefixes A , AB , and ABC . The losses after X cannot teach the model how to continue from the correct prefixes A , AB , and ABC , and therefore do not advance learning along the target code trajectory. Training must first correct the initial error from X to A before the later target positions become exposed, so injection proceeds front to back. Teacher forcing avoids this sequential dependency: by supplying ABCD during training, it places losses on the target prefixes A , AB , and ABC in the same update. The bottom-right panel of Figure 1 shows this coverage bottleneck most clearly: among the forward-KL conditions, gold-prefix training remains near ceiling across the full range of code lengths, whereas on-policy recall collapses beyond a few dozen tokens. Thus, the more document-specific tokens an answer requires, the greater the disadvantage of on-policy rollouts relative to teacher forcing. Read left to right, the top row of Figure 1 shows how the two bottlenecks accumulate. Moving from digits L8 to base36 L32 raises target difficulty and stalls both reverse-KL variants, while both forward-KL variants still reach the teacher ceiling. At essentially the same difficulty ( 185 185 versus 184 184 nats), lengthening the code from 23 23 to 64 64 tokens then collapses on-policy forward KL while PD remains strong, isolating rollout coverage. Finally, reducing difficulty to 78 78 nats at the same 64 64 -token length restores on-policy forward KL near the teacher ceiling, showing that difficulty shifts where the coverage wall appears but does not replace length as a distinct axis. sections.heading: 5 Adaptive-Policy Distillation
sections.text: The analysis above suggests a selective remedy. At document-specific positions where the student assigns little probability to teacher-preferred tokens, the objective should shift toward forward KL to restore the missing gradient, while the rollout should shift toward the teacher to keep later target positions reachable. Applying these interventions everywhere, however, would discard OPD’s main advantage: training on the student-generated states encountered at inference. We therefore propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), which intervenes only where teacher and student disagree and otherwise reduces to OPD. APD implements this adaptation with a single gating signal: the per-token divergence between teacher and student at the current state, κ t = D KL ( π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ∥ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ) , \kappa_{t}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big), (4) from which the gate g t = 1 − e − κ t / τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) g_{t}=1-e^{-\kappa_{t}/\tau}\in[0,1) (5) is formed, where τ \tau is the method’s single hyperparameter and κ t \kappa_{t} is treated as a constant during backpropagation. The temperature τ \tau controls the gate’s selectivity: for a fixed divergence, increasing τ \tau keeps g t g_{t} closer to zero, so moderate disagreements continue to use OPD and only large mismatches receive substantial teacher intervention. Which mismatches open the gate is determined by the direction of κ t \kappa_{t} . Because teacher and student share weights and differ only in whether they receive the document, probability mass that is high under the teacher but low under the student identifies tokens likely to carry document-specific information missing from the student. The forward divergence D KL ( π T ∥ π θ ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{T}\|\pi_{\theta}) weights precisely this teacher-preferred mass. Accordingly, g t g_{t} is open ( g t → 1 g_{t}\to 1 ) at large teacher–student coverage gaps and remains near closed ( g t ≈ 0 g_{t}\approx 0 ) when the divergence is small relative to τ \tau , allowing moderate differences to be handled by OPD. The gate intervenes twice, with the same signal. During rollout, the next token is drawn from the per-token mixture y t ∼ m t = ( 1 − g t ) π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) + g t π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) , y_{t}\sim m_{t}=(1-g_{t})\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})+g_{t}\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t}), (6) so generation remains effectively on-policy wherever κ t \kappa_{t} is small relative to τ \tau , and shifts substantially toward the teacher only at high-divergence positions; no token is ever discretely handed over. In the loss, the same gate blends the two KL directions at every state of the resulting rollout: ℒ APD = 𝔼 y ∼ m [ ∑ t ( 1 − g t ) D KL ( π θ ∥ π T ) + g t D KL ( π T ∥ π θ ) ] , \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{APD}}=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim m}\Big[\sum_{t}&(1-g_{t})\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T}\big)\\[-2.0pt] &+g_{t}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{T}\|\pi_{\theta}\big)\Big],\end{split} (7) with all divergences evaluated at s t s_{t} . APD uses only the teacher logits already required by OPD, with no labels, verifier, or additional teacher evaluations. The gate and mixture add only elementwise operations, so the FLOP count is unchanged and matched timing runs show wall-clock parity with OPD when memory is sufficient (Appendix C.2 ). The added cost is memory: the teacher generates alongside the rollout, so its KV cache remains resident during training rollout generation.

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate document knowledge injection on two generative QA benchmarks requiring document-specific content: QASPER ( Dasigi et al., 2021 ) , information-seeking QA over full NLP papers (up to ∼ \sim 9k tokens; 16,384-token context), scored on answerable questions with token-level Answer-F1 and its precision and recall components; and BioASQ ( Krithara et al., 2023 ) , biomedical factoid QA over full PMC articles, scored by strict and lenient accuracy and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) over up to five ranked answers. Dataset details are given in Appendix B . For each benchmark, we use twenty documents as separate injection units: every method is trained independently on QA about each document and evaluated closed-book. All methods, including APD, are trained on two base models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025a ) in non-thinking mode, referred to below as Llama-3.1 and Qwen3. We train every method for 10 epochs with global batch size 64, AdamW ( 10 − 5 10^{-5} ), and seed 42, and evaluate the final checkpoint. All other training, rollout, and decoding settings are held fixed across all methods. For APD, τ \tau is selected once per model on ten held-out BioASQ development documents and used for both datasets. Training details and the selection procedure are given in Appendix C . Tables report per-method means over documents (absolute scores). Since every method trains on the same document set, significance is assessed with paired t t -tests across documents (Appendix C.2 ).

sections.heading: 6.1 Training and Evaluation Data
sections.text: Because each benchmark provides only one to six questions per document, we construct document-specific training and evaluation sets from the source documents. For training, Qwen3-235B generates questions from each document, and the document-conditioned base model generates the corresponding answers, yielding 0.6 0.6 – 1.3 1.3 k QA pairs per document. For evaluation, we generate a held-out set of approximately 100 questions and reference answers per document using GPT-5.4 ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , with the benchmark’s human-written examples provided as demonstrations to preserve its question and answer style. To validate the evaluation set, we compare closed-book and open-book performance of the untrained model. Providing the source document increases QASPER F1 from .148 .148 to .764 .764 and BioASQ MRR from .151 .151 to .748 .748 for Llama-3.1, and from .157 .157 to .701 .701 and .151 .151 to .713 .713 for Qwen3, indicating that the generated questions are answerable from the document but largely inaccessible without it. The generation procedure and all prompts are given in Appendices B.2 and G .

sections.heading: 6.2 Baselines
sections.text: SFT and PD generate a corpus from the teacher once before training and reuse it in every epoch. APD instead draws tokens from the teacher wherever its gate opens, so its teacher samples change at every step. A fixed corpus thus repeats the same teacher answers in every epoch, whereas resampling adds new teacher information each epoch. Prior token-level methods similar to APD compare against fixed-corpus or student-rollout baselines, but not against a resampled teacher corpus ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Koo et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2025 ) . To separate the effect of resampling, we group the baselines by this property, as in Table 1 .

sections.heading: No teacher resampling.
sections.text: Besides SFT and PD, this group includes methods that generate no teacher samples at all, such as OPD. It also includes GKD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , which mixes the fixed corpus and student rollouts at a fixed rate ( λ = 0.5 \lambda{=}0.5 ) under the Jensen–Shannon divergence, and ToDi ( Jung et al., 2025 ) , which blends forward and reverse KL per vocabulary entry on the fixed corpus.

sections.heading: Teacher resampled during training.
sections.text: We refer to PD with teacher responses resampled at every step instead of a fixed corpus as Resampled PD . It is equivalent to APD with the gate fully open ( g t ≡ 1 g_{t}\equiv 1 ). Since injection depends on the teacher exposing content the student cannot produce (§ 4 ), resampling’s advantage over PD grows with the number of training epochs (Appendix E.1 ). We also evaluate resampled counterparts of SFT and GKD (Appendix E.2 ). Four published methods also resample the teacher during training: SKD ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , which replaces student tokens outside the teacher’s top- K K and applies forward KL; SWITCH ( Koo et al., 2025 ) , which lets the teacher intervene when token probabilities diverge; AdaSwitch ( Peng et al., 2025 ) , which switches to the teacher once the divergence exceeds a moving threshold; and MiniLLM ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , which mixes the teacher into every token at a fixed rate and optimizes sequence-level reverse KL by policy gradient. Baseline-specific hyperparameters follow the original papers. sections.heading: 6.3 Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 compares APD with the baselines on both models and datasets. We discuss the primary metrics, F1 for QASPER and MRR for BioASQ. Appendix D adds standard deviations and significance tests for every metric. We call a difference significant when a two-sided paired t t -test over the twenty documents gives p < .10 p<.10 , that is, at the 90 % 90\% confidence level.

sections.heading: On-policy distillation falls below every fixed-corpus method.
sections.text: OPD samples only from the student and trains with reverse KL. In all four settings it scores below every method that trains on a fixed teacher corpus, by .050 .050 to .084 .084 against the lowest of them. Under information asymmetry, distilling on the student’s own rollouts thus injects less than imitating answers that the teacher generated once before training, as our analysis in § 4 predicts.

sections.heading: Resampling the teacher helps with forward KL.
sections.text: The methods that resample the teacher with a forward-KL term in the loss, Resampled PD, SKD, AdaSwitch, and APD, are on average above the fixed-corpus baselines in every setting, by .031 .031 to .074 .074 . MiniLLM and SWITCH also resample the teacher but do not gain from it. Both train with reverse-KL objectives and fall below every fixed-corpus method. This is the pattern of the testbed in § 4 , where the source of the training sequences matters only once the loss is forward KL. Under information asymmetry, seeing teacher sequences repeatedly is thus not enough. The loss must raise the student’s low token probabilities.

sections.heading: APD is the best method in every setting.
sections.text: APD scores highest in all four settings, above the resampled forward-KL baselines as well as the fixed-corpus ones. Adding its gate raises OPD by .140 .140 to .168 .168 in every setting ( t ≥ 6.5 t\geq 6.5 ). SKD and AdaSwitch, whose rules decide token by token whether the student or the teacher generates, are on par with Resampled PD in three settings and significantly below it on Llama-3.1 BioASQ ( − .029 -.029 and − .043 -.043 MRR), and Appendix C.4 examines how their sampling rules behave in our setting. APD, in contrast, is significantly above Resampled PD in three of the four settings. More broadly, it is significantly above every baseline in every setting except three comparisons on BioASQ, against Resampled PD for Llama-3.1 and against SKD and AdaSwitch for Qwen3, which it still exceeds by .016 .016 to .022 .022 MRR.

sections.heading: The loss comes first, then sampling.
sections.text: Table 2 sets the sampling and loss axes independently. With reverse KL, every sampling choice stays at the level of OPD ( .309 .309 – .324 .324 ). Letting the teacher generate does not help as long as the loss cannot raise the student’s low token probabilities. For every sampling choice, forward KL raises MRR over reverse KL by .126 .126 to .171 .171 , and the gated loss raises it further by .007 .007 to .021 .021 . Once the loss is forward KL or gated, sampling also orders the cells, with student sampling lowest, teacher sampling next, and gated sampling highest. Gating is thus the best choice on each axis once reverse KL is excluded, and full APD, which gates both, scores highest ( .486 .486 ). This matches the pattern of the testbed (§ 4 ) and of the main results.

sections.heading: The gate temperature.
sections.text: Table 3 varies τ \tau between OPD, where the gate is always closed ( τ → ∞ \tau{\to}\infty ), and Resampled PD, where it is always open ( τ → 0 \tau{\to}0 ). MRR rises steeply as soon as the gate begins to open. At τ = 10 \tau=10 , where the teacher contributes only 2 2 – 3 % 3\% of the sampling mass, MRR rises from .324 .324 to .444 .444 , and at τ = 3 \tau=3 , with about 6 % 6\% , to .469 .469 . In every setting, τ = 10 \tau=10 already recovers 52 52 – 74 % 74\% of the gain of the selected τ \tau over OPD, and τ = 3 \tau=3 recovers 77 77 – 98 % 98\% . Intervening at a small fraction of tokens thus removes most of the deficit of OPD, and additional teacher mass refines the rest.

sections.heading: Where versus how much.
sections.text: To separate where the gate opens from how much teacher mass it injects, the last row of Table 3 replaces the per-token gate on both axes with a constant gate of 0.25 0.25 , matched to the average gate of APD ( .26 .26 ). This constant gate reaches .445 .445 , significantly below APD ( − .042 -.042 , t = − 3.67 t=-3.67 ) and also below Resampled PD. It does no better than τ = 10 \tau=10 ( .444 .444 ), which injects about a tenth of that mass at the positions of largest divergence. Figure 2 shows how widely the gate opens. At τ = 3 \tau=3 , the gate exceeds 0.5 0.5 at only 3.8 % 3.8\% of tokens before training and 1.6 % 1.6\% after, yet APD still reaches .469 .469 MRR, close to the .486 .486 of τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 and far above OPD. At τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 , the gate opens at 51.7 % 51.7\% of tokens before training and narrows to 15.1 % 15.1\% during training. Most of the gain of APD therefore comes from a small set of high-divergence positions, and the wider opening at τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 adds the rest. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We analyzed why on-policy distillation becomes inefficient for knowledge injection, identifying weak reverse-KL supervision and limited student-rollout coverage. Based on this analysis, we proposed APD, which selectively adapts both the loss and rollout where teacher–student divergence is large. Our experiments show that the two failures are addressed in order, since sampling from the teacher helps only once the loss can raise the low token probabilities of the student, and that intervening at a small set of high-divergence positions already removes most of the deficit of OPD.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We study knowledge injection, where the teacher holds information that the student cannot infer, so their distributions differ sharply on the content to be injected. We therefore do not test general distillation, where the student already produces a distribution close to that of the teacher, and other bottlenecks may dominate there. Our experiments cover two 8B backbones and two document-QA benchmarks, so how the two bottlenecks change with model scale and domain remains open. Most real-data evaluation questions and references are model-generated. Open-book checks and the smaller human-written question sets support their validity, but generator artifacts may still affect absolute scores or method rankings. Our comparisons measure learning efficiency at fixed budgets—400 steps in the testbed and 10 epochs on real documents—rather than asymptotic injection capacity, and additional compute or method-specific tuning could alter the ordering. The controlled key–code testbed deliberately removes linguistic structure and uses one training configuration, so it isolates the two mechanisms but does not establish how frequently they dominate natural knowledge injection. Finally, APD has similar FLOPs and wall-clock time to OPD when memory is sufficient, but because the teacher must stay resident during generation, it cannot offload one model while the other runs, which may limit scaling to larger models or longer contexts.

sections.heading: Appendix B Datasets
sections.text: All documents, questions, and answers used in our experiments are in English.

sections.heading: B.1 Benchmarks and Metrics
sections.text: We use QASPER and BioASQ because they provide long, knowledge-intensive documents in specialized fields (science and medicine), human-written question–answer pairs that can serve as demonstrations for generating evaluation questions, and established metrics.

sections.heading: QASPER.
sections.text: QASPER contains information-seeking questions about NLP papers. Each document is a full paper of up to approximately 9 9 k tokens and fits within our 16,384 16{,}384 -token context window. Answer-F1 is token overlap between the generated and gold answer after standard normalization, maximized over gold references. We also report precision and recall because closed-book answers vary in length: recall tracks whether the injected content surfaces, while precision tracks whether it is stated without padding. We score only answerable questions because success on an unanswerable question measures abstention rather than retention of document content.

sections.heading: BioASQ.
sections.text: BioASQ contains biomedical factoid questions, each paired with the full text of the PMC article that answers it. The model returns up to five ranked candidates: strict accuracy requires the top candidate to exactly match the gold answer or a listed synonym, lenient accuracy accepts a match anywhere in the list, and MRR uses the rank of the first correct candidate.

sections.heading: B.2 Data Generation

Every unit carries three question sets: the benchmark’s human-written questions (two to six per QASPER paper, 72 72 in total over the test units of which 62 62 are answerable; one per BioASQ article, 20 20 in total), a training set, and a generated evaluation set. sections.heading: Training questions.
sections.text: Questions are generated by Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 at temperature 0.9 0.9 . The document is first split along its own markdown structure into passages, and the generator is then queried at three scopes: single , one passage at a time (target 2,400 2{,}400 questions per document); cross , a sliding group of passages with the requirement that an answer draw on two or more of them ( 1,200 1{,}200 ); and full , the whole document, for questions about its overall aim and central findings ( 450 450 ). Each request asks for a number of questions proportional to the passage length (between 2 2 and 15 15 ) and returns a JSON array of question/evidence pairs, the evidence being a verbatim quote supporting the answer. The system prompt is domain-neutral: it says only “article”, names no field, and is identical for both datasets. It requires the questions to be self-contained, forbidding meta-reference to the prompt, and to vary widely in form. The collected questions are then deduplicated per document by MinHash LSH over character 3-grams at Jaccard threshold 0.45 0.45 , and any question that still matches a list of meta-reference phrases, such as “the passage” or “the author”, is dropped. Because the hashing procedure is approximate, some near-duplicates may remain in the training set.

sections.heading: Training answers.
sections.text: Answers are generated by the base model itself, greedily (temperature 0 0 , up to 512 512 tokens), from the document in a <context> block followed by the question and with no system prompt: this is exactly the input the teacher π T \pi_{T} receives during training (§ 3 ). Thus, the off-policy targets and the on-policy teacher use the same checkpoint and document-conditioned input. Empty answers are dropped, along with the occasional runaway generation, leaving between 616 616 and 1,286 1{,}286 QA pairs per test unit, of which about two thirds are single-scope, most of the rest cross-passage, and a small remainder full-document.

sections.heading: Evaluation set.
sections.text: The evaluation set is generated per document by GPT-5.4 through its API, in a single call supplying the article, up to five of that document’s human-written (question, answer) pairs as style examples, and a request for 100 100 diverse, non-redundant pairs, each naming a specific entity and answerable only from the article. For BioASQ the prompt additionally constrains the answer to a single named entity or short canonical term: the factoid metric is exact match against a reference string, so a descriptive gold phrase would make the score reflect phrasing rather than knowledge. Returned pairs are retained only if the answer occurs in the article and the question has a word-level Jaccard overlap below 0.45 0.45 with every question already accepted for the same document. Unlike the approximate hashing used for the training set, this exact comparison leaves no pair above the threshold. Between 78 78 and 116 116 questions per test unit survive. Table 4 shows examples drawn from all three sets of one unit per dataset.

sections.heading: C.1 Synthetic Testbed
sections.text: The key–code testbed of § 4 uses Qwen3-1.7B as both teacher and student, with the teacher frozen and reading the key–value document. Every cell shares one configuration: global batch 64 64 , 400 400 steps, learning rate 5 × 10 − 6 5{\times}10^{-6} , seed 42 42 . Closed-book recall is measured by exact string match over the N = 64 N{=}64 keys.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Student and teacher are the same base checkpoint, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen3-8B. The teacher is frozen and reads the document, whereas the student never does. For Qwen3, thinking mode is disabled throughout via the chat template. Parameters are held in BF16 with FP32 optimizer states under DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 across two B200 GPUs. We use AdamW (learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , weight decay 0.01 0.01 ), gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 , a cosine schedule with warmup ratio 0.03 0.03 , and a maximum sequence length of 16,384 16{,}384 tokens, which covers the longest document in either corpus. The global batch size of 64 64 is reached by gradient accumulation. Every method is trained for 10 10 epochs and evaluated at the final checkpoint. All KL and Jensen–Shannon divergences are computed over the full vocabulary. No top- k k truncation is applied to these objectives.

sections.heading: Rollouts.
sections.text: On-policy methods generate with vLLM colocated with the trainer on the same two GPUs, and the engine’s weights are refreshed from the current student at every step, so the rollouts are on-policy in the strict sense. Completions are capped at 512 512 tokens. Rollouts are sampled at temperature 1.0 1.0 with no nucleus or top- k k truncation, except for SKD and AdaSwitch, which use the sampling settings of their original papers (Appendix C.4 ). APD additionally maintains a second engine for the teacher. The teacher reads the document and the student does not. At every position, both engines compute next-token distributions on the same prefix, the gate of Eq. 4 mixes them, and the sampled token is appended to both. Both engines run with chunked prefill and prefix caching enabled. These change how the forward pass is scheduled, not what it returns. Table 5 compares the training cost of OPD and APD. The rollouts of APD take longer because the teacher decodes alongside the student, but APD reuses these teacher logits in the loss instead of running a separate teacher forward pass. In addition, the rollouts of APD are 15 15 – 33 % 33\% shorter than those of OPD, as they are partly sampled from the teacher, which reads the document. Its step time is therefore comparable to or lower than that of OPD. The cost is that both engines must stay resident while APD generates, whereas OPD can generate with the student and score with the teacher in separate phases and offload whichever model is idle. sections.heading: C.3 Temperature Selection
sections.text: For each model, we select τ \tau for APD once from { 0.01 , 0.1 , 0.3 , 1 , 3 , 10 } \{0.01,0.1,0.3,1,3,10\} on ten BioASQ development documents that are disjoint from the twenty test documents, and use the selected value for both datasets. The training and evaluation sets of these development documents are built by the same pipeline (Appendix B.2 ). We train APD on each development document with each τ \tau and choose the value with the highest mean strict accuracy. Table 6 lists the development scores, and the selected values, τ = 0.3 \tau=0.3 for Llama-3.1 and τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 for Qwen3, are the highest on all three metrics.

sections.heading: C.4 Baseline Settings
sections.text: Every baseline uses the method-specific hyperparameters of its original paper, whereas the training setup shared by all methods (optimizer, learning rate, number of epochs, batch size, and maximum length; Appendix C.2 ) is ours. In their original papers, most on-policy baselines first fine-tune the student with SFT and then distill into it. We instead distill into the student without this step, to measure injection under the largest information asymmetry between student and teacher. Appendix E.5 shows that APD remains the best method when every method is first fine-tuned with SFT. Below we describe the baselines whose settings need comment.

sections.heading: GKD.
sections.text: We run GKD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) with a student-data fraction of λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , which the authors call mixed sampling, and the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence with β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 . The original work treats both as task-dependent hyperparameters and tunes them per task. We did not repeat that search for every setting, but our ablation on Llama-3.1 and BioASQ (Table 2 ) covers part of it, varying the sampling source and the direction of the KL divergence, though not the Jensen–Shannon divergence.

sections.heading: MiniLLM.
sections.text: We follow the official implementation of MiniLLM ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , including teacher-mixed sampling with α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , single-step regularization, and length normalization, with two differences. We omit the auxiliary language-modeling loss on a pretraining corpus, which our setting does not have. We perform one policy update per rollout instead of four, as for the other on-policy methods. sections.heading: SKD.
sections.text: We use the original hyperparameters of Xu et al. (2025) , K = 25 K=25 , which the authors fix without parameter search, and their sampling settings, temperature 0.5 0.5 with top- p p 0.5 0.5 for the student and temperature 0.2 0.2 for the teacher. In their setting, where a larger teacher distills into a smaller student, the teacher replaces 40.9 % 40.9\% of student tokens early in training and about 5 % 5\% later. In our setting, the teacher replaces far fewer tokens. At K = 25 K=25 , it replaces at most 1.0 % 1.0\% of tokens before any update, and this falls to 0.2 0.2 – 0.3 % 0.3\% during training. At K = 5 K=5 , the most aggressive value in the range the authors recommend, it replaces at most 4.6 % 4.6\% . Only below that range, at K = 2 K=2 and K = 1 K=1 , does the rate rise to 12 12 – 32 % 32\% , which is still below the initial rate of the original paper (Table 8 ). This follows from our setting, in which student and teacher are the same model and differ only in whether the document is in the prompt, so 81 81 – 87 % 87\% of student-sampled tokens are the teacher’s most likely token and 98 98 – 99.5 % 99.5\% are within its top 25 25 . Its rollouts are therefore close to those of student sampling with forward KL, the corresponding cell of Table 2 , and the two score .435 .435 and .450 .450 MRR on Llama-3.1 and BioASQ. Nevertheless, a more aggressive K K does not help. Training with K = 5 K=5 leaves MRR on Llama-3.1 and BioASQ unchanged within noise ( − .008 -.008 , t = − 0.78 t=-0.78 ), so we keep the original value.

sections.heading: AdaSwitch.
sections.text: We use the original hyperparameters of Peng et al. (2025) , k = 3 k=3 and a window of L = 10 L=10 tokens, with its sampling settings. In our setting, 82–90% of rollouts switch to the teacher, on average around the 16th generated token, and the teacher then generates the rest of the sequence. The teacher therefore produces 76–94% of rollout tokens throughout training, the opposite of SKD.

sections.heading: E.4 Degenerate Outputs

On BioASQ it is an entity name from the article, and all such models were trained on the same document. Each method yields one trained model per test document, and we count a trained model as degenerate when more than 30 % 30\% of its answers to its document’s questions are the same string after lowercasing and removing trailing punctuation. Table 13 counts degenerate models. sections.text: We first give the single-passage question-generation prompt. The cross-passage and full-document scopes use the same prompt with the passage description and rules 2–4 replaced as noted below. Questions: system prompt (single-passage scope) You curate a question dataset about the given article. Each question’s subject is the article’s content --- its facts, claims, findings or events, entities, values, relationships, sequences, and outcomes. You are shown one passage from a longer article; treat it as a factual source. Questions must stand alone. Rules: 1. Self-contained questions --- STRICTLY no meta-reference to your prompt. A reader who has read the whole article but does NOT see your prompt must be able to answer. Forbidden phrasings include but are not limited to: "the excerpt", "the passage", "the article", "the source", "the text", "the section", "the piece", "the paragraph", "this excerpt", "this passage", "this article", "in the passage", "in the excerpt", "according to the excerpt", "according to the passage", "the author writes / says / states / argues / describes". Rephrase by naming the subject directly. Bad: "What does the article say about Dole?" Good: "What did Dole charge the New York Times with?" --- questions read like trivia about the topic, not like reading-comprehension prompts. 2. Scope each question so the answer is fully determined by facts in the passage you are shown. 3. Vary the angle: factual lookup, what/which/who/where/when/how, comparison, cause, condition, mechanism, outcome. 4. Evidence: 1-2 sentence verbatim quote from the passage that supports the answer. 5. Write all questions in English. 6. FORM DIVERSITY: vary the question FORM widely --- beyond what/which/how, also use comparison, ordering/sequence, cause-effect, fill-in-the-blank, true/false, ’which is NOT’, counting, multi-step reasoning, and multiple-choice (3-4 options). 7. ANSWER-FORMAT CUES: for SOME questions whose answer is a short exact fact, embed an explicit answer instruction inside the question itself --- e.g. ’answer in N words or fewer’, ’give only the short answer, no explanation’, ’reply yes or no’, ’answer as a comma-separated list’. Leave others open (why/how) for a fuller answer. Aim for a real spread of expected answer lengths across the set. Output format: JSON array with items of shape {"question": "...", "evidence": "..."}. Favor comparison, sequencing, cause-and-effect, or contrast across sections. 4. Evidence: 1-2 sentence verbatim quote from the sections that supports the answer. At full -document scope the subject becomes “the article as a whole — its overall aim, central findings or events, main claims, big-picture relationships”, and the model is shown the full article. Full-document scope: replaces rules 2–4 2. Favor big-picture questions requiring whole-article understanding: the overall aim, central findings, the main comparison, the conclusion. 3. Prefer questions that cannot be answered from a single paragraph. 4. Evidence: 1-2 sentence verbatim quote that supports the answer. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2611.00852v1 [cs.CL] 31 Oct 2026 Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry Hojun Cho Affiliation: KAIST Email: hojun.cho@kaist.ac.kr Kang Eun Jeon Affiliation: DGIST Email: kejeon@dgist.ac.kr Jaegul Choo Affiliation: KAIST Email: jchoo@kaist.ac.kr Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model’s behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher–student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6 % 54.6\% , achieving the best scores of 0.558 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 0.486 MRR on BioASQ. 1 Introduction Many LLM applications repeatedly answer questions using the same long documents, such as technical manuals, scientific literature, legal texts, or organization-specific knowledge. Placing those documents in the inference context is effective ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , but repeatedly processing them wastes computation and context-window capacity. Context distillation instead injects a fixed document into model parameters: the document-conditioned model teaches the same model without the document, enabling closed-book inference without a stronger teacher, gold labels, or a verifier ( Askell et al., 2021 ; Snell et al., 2022 ; Kujanpää et al., 2025 ) . Recent distillation methods increasingly replace off-policy teacher-generated data with on-policy supervision of the student’s own sequences ( Song and Zheng, 2026 ) ; training on states encountered at inference reduces train–inference mismatch and often improves behavior transfer ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , motivating the same extension to context distillation ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . When context distillation is used for knowledge injection, however, we observe a surprising reversal: across two document-QA datasets, pure on-policy context distillation (OPD) is consistently weaker than off-policy distillation. Prior work separately points to weak reverse-KL supervision outside the student’s effective support ( Minka, 2005 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and inadequate rollout coverage of teacher-preferred behavior ( Lazaridis et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . We ask how these two limitations interact when the teacher’s only advantage is information absent from the student’s input. We study this interaction in a controlled context-distillation testbed whose documents contain random key–code mappings unavailable from the model’s prior knowledge. We vary two properties of the codes independently: token-level unpredictability and length. For each setting, we run the full generation-source × \times KL-direction grid. The results show how properties of the knowledge to be injected control the interaction between the two limitations. Reverse KL fails regardless of generation source, making the objective the primary bottleneck; once forward KL restores the token-level signal, student rollouts become limiting as the codes grow longer. Thus, under the information asymmetry of knowledge injection, OPD is least efficient exactly where the document contributes the most content the student cannot infer on its own. The implication is selective rather than global: OPD should be retained where the teacher–student mismatch is modest, with intervention reserved for positions where document-specific information creates a large coverage gap. We therefore propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), which uses a per-token divergence gate to jointly adapt the rollout and objective. At high-divergence positions, APD shifts sampling toward the teacher and the loss toward forward KL; otherwise, the gate remains nearly closed and training stays effectively on-policy. As the student learns, the divergence falls and both interventions shrink toward OPD. APD requires neither gold answers nor a verifier, yet raises OPD from below every off-policy baseline to parity with the strongest of them on our benchmarks. Our contributions are as follows: • Using a controlled context-distillation testbed, we show how token-level unpredictability and sequence length expose distinct OPD bottlenecks along KL direction and generation source (§ 4 ). • We propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose reversible per-token divergence gate jointly adapts sampling and KL direction without gold answers or a verifier (§ 5 ). • Using real documents, ablations reproduce the testbed’s bottleneck hierarchy and show that intervening at only a small fraction of tokens recovers most of the gain (§ 6 ). 2 Related Work 2.1 Knowledge Injection via Distillation Ye et al. (2026) apply on-policy context distillation to system prompts and solution traces, whereas we study the internalization of document-specific knowledge unavailable in the student’s input. Closest to our setting, GATES distills from document-conditioned tutor traces using consensus gating ( Stein et al., 2026 ) , MixSD combines conditioned and unconditioned predictions at a fixed ratio ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and EDGE-OPD guides student rollouts with a fixed teacher mixture while masking the loss using binary teacher evidence ( Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) . Beyond distillation, document knowledge can also be injected by synthetic continued pretraining ( Yang et al., 2025b ) . These interventions reflect a broader difficulty of on-policy distillation: teacher-preferred content with low student probability is unlikely to be effectively learned. Prior analyses show that student rollouts rarely reach such content ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) , while some methods exclude teacher preferences outside the student’s effective support as unteachable ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . In knowledge injection, however, these low-support tokens are precisely what must be learned. Related work further shows that forward and reverse KL can behave differently under finite training budgets despite sharing the same optimum ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and that prefix source and KL direction can be varied independently ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . We extend this analysis to knowledge injection and use a single adaptive, reversible per-token gate to control both prefix generation and the distillation objective, rather than relying on fixed mixtures or hard masks. 2.2 Bridging the Teacher–Student Mismatch Token-level remedies for teacher–student mismatch fall into three groups. Sampling-side methods replace student tokens outside the teacher’s top- K K (SKD) ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , let the teacher intervene when token probabilities diverge (SWITCH) ( Koo et al., 2025 ) , or switch to teacher generation after a moving divergence threshold (AdaSwitch) ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . Schedule-side methods interpolate an intermediate teacher (TAID) ( Shing et al., 2025 ) or anneal a global forward-to-reverse KL mixture with a coverage-based brake (CADENCE) ( Kumar and Jha, 2026 ) . DistiLLM adaptively schedules student-generated data ( Ko et al., 2024 ) , while DistiLLM-2 pairs different losses with teacher- versus student-generated data ( Ko et al., 2025 ) . Loss-side methods blend KL directions per token via probability-ratio weights on fixed data ( Jung et al., 2025 ) or mask unteachable tokens ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Each intervenes on sampling, scheduling, or loss alone; APD instead uses one state-dependent per-token signal for both the sampling mix and KL direction. Bottom: final recall as a function of per-token branching at fixed code length (left) and answer length across cells (right). Solid/dashed lines denote forward/reverse KL, faint markers are individual cells, and lines in the bottom-right panel are binned means. 3 Problem Setup We consider a self-distillation problem where the teacher is the frozen base model conditioned on the document, hence any teacher–student difference is purely informational ( Stein et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Lazaridis et al., 2026 ) . Let d d be a document to internalize and x x a question about it. An autoregressive model defines π ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = ∏ t π ⁡ ( y t ∣ s t ) \pi(y\mid x)=\prod_{t}\pi(y_{t}\mid s_{t}) over responses y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) , where s t = ( x , y < t ) s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) denotes the state at step t t . The teacher is the frozen base model with the document in its context, π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) = π 0 ( ⋅ ∣ d , x , y < t ) \pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})=\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid d,x,y_{<t}) . The student π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) never sees the document and starts from the same base model without it, π 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) \pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) . The goal is for the student to reproduce the teacher’s document-conditioned behavior without reading d d . In the distillation family studied here, the student is trained against the teacher’s full next-token distribution rather than against sampled tokens as hard labels: the loss is a per-token divergence D D between student and teacher, summed over the states of a sampled response ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Song and Zheng, 2026 ) . Writing ρ \rho for the distribution of y y , the family is ℒ ⁡ ( θ ) = 𝔼 y ∼ ρ [ ∑ t D ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) , π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ) ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\theta)={}&\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\rho}\Big[\sum_{t}D\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big)\Big].\end{split} (1) Recipes within it differ along two axes. The first is where the loss is evaluated : the generation source ρ \rho is either a fixed corpus of teacher-generated responses, independent of the current student, on which the student is teacher-forced ( off-policy ), or the student’s own rollouts, resampled as the student changes ( on-policy ). The second is which divergence is minimized : D D is either the forward KL D KL ( π T ∥ π θ ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{T}\|\pi_{\theta}) or the reverse KL D KL ( π θ ∥ π T ) D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T}) . Of the four resulting combinations, two are the recipes used in practice. PD (per-token off-policy distillation) applies forward KL on teacher-forced states, i.e. word-level KD ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . OPD applies token-level reverse KL to the document-conditioned teacher on the student’s own rollouts ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . The remaining two, reverse KL on teacher-forced states (off-rev) and forward KL on student rollouts (on-fwd), are rarely used on their own: the two choices travel together in practice ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . One further reference, SFT , falls outside Eq. 1 altogether: it fits sampled teacher tokens as hard targets without consuming the teacher logits. 4 Why On-Policy Distillation Fails to Inject Knowledge Injection concerns knowledge the student does not have, so measuring it cleanly calls for a target the student genuinely cannot know. We build one synthetically. The context is a key–value store: a fixed document listing N = 64 N{=}64 lines of the form “ The code for {key} is {code}. ” The codes are drawn at random, so the document is the only place they exist and no amount of prior knowledge substitutes for reading it. For each key, we ask the probe “ What is the code for { key } ? Output only the code, nothing else. ” The teacher and student share the same base model, but only the teacher receives the key–value store as document context in its system turn. The resulting asymmetry is therefore purely informational. To answer correctly, the student must internalize the key → \to code mapping in its weights. Closed-book exact-match recall over the N N keys therefore directly measures how many mappings have been successfully injected. To test how the form of the knowledge affects how readily it is internalized, we vary the alphabet size ( | Σ | ∈ { 2 , 10 , 16 , 36 , 62 } |\Sigma|\in\{2,10,16,36,62\} ) and code length ( L ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } L\in\{2,4,8,16,32,64,128\} ). These two variables control how unpredictable each code is and how many tokens must be learned in sequence. We quantify each cell’s difficulty by the mean teacher-forced, closed-book negative log-probability of its gold codes under the base model, − log ⁡ p base ​ ( code ) -\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(\text{code}) . The resulting values range from 21 21 to 632 632 nats. This controlled construction lets us vary target difficulty and length separately, which is not possible with real-data benchmarks. On this grid we run all four cells of § 3 , with SFT as a hard-target reference and all other settings held fixed across cells. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix C.1 . Where the signal vanishes. OPD minimizes the reverse KL at states the student itself visits: ℒ OPD = 𝔼 y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ ∑ t D KL ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ∥ π T ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) ) ] . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}={}&\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\\ &\Big[\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\big)\Big].\end{split} (2) Equation 2 combines two choices that can bottleneck injection: the reverse-KL objective and the student-generated state distribution. The full generation-source × \times KL-direction grid in Figure 1 separates their effects. We first examine the KL direction. Across the figure, both reverse-KL variants lag behind their forward-KL counterparts regardless of generation source. Even in the easiest top-left cell, both forward-KL runs saturate within 100 100 steps, whereas both reverse-KL runs are still climbing at step 400 400 . To see why, hold the sampled state s s fixed and consider the gradient with respect to the student logit of a token a a : π θ ( a ∣ s ) [ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) π T ​ ( a ∣ s ) − D KL ( π θ ∥ π T ) ] . \begin{split}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\Big[&\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{T}(a\mid s)}\\ &-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{T}\big)\Big].\end{split} (3) The gradient is scaled by π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) \pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) and therefore vanishes as π θ ​ ( a ∣ s ) → 0 \pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\to 0 . Reverse KL thus provides little first-order signal for raising a low-probability token, which is its zero-forcing property ( Minka, 2005 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Jung et al., 2025 ) . A derivation and its assumptions are given in Appendix A . Document-specific tokens are precisely the tokens that the student initially considers unlikely and injection must raise. The bottom-left panel makes this dependence visible. At fixed length, a wider alphabet makes each target symbol less probable under the student; as Equation 3 predicts, the resulting reduction in gradient magnitude increasingly prevents both reverse-KL variants from learning the codes. Both forward-KL conditions remain at ceiling, while the near-overlap of the two reverse-KL conditions shows that the generation source makes little difference in this regime. The second bottleneck lies in the student-generated state distribution. On-policy training places the loss on whatever the student generated. But the student has never read the document, so at the positions that carry document-specific content it has nothing to produce the right token from; these are exactly the positions at which its rollouts leave the target. For example, suppose the target code is ABCD , but the student samples X as its first symbol. Every subsequent loss is then evaluated at prefixes beginning with X , rather than at the target prefixes A , AB , and ABC . The losses after X cannot teach the model how to continue from the correct prefixes A , AB , and ABC , and therefore do not advance learning along the target code trajectory. Training must first correct the initial error from X to A before the later target positions become exposed, so injection proceeds front to back. Teacher forcing avoids this sequential dependency: by supplying ABCD during training, it places losses on the target prefixes A , AB , and ABC in the same update. The bottom-right panel of Figure 1 shows this coverage bottleneck most clearly: among the forward-KL conditions, gold-prefix training remains near ceiling across the full range of code lengths, whereas on-policy recall collapses beyond a few dozen tokens. Thus, the more document-specific tokens an answer requires, the greater the disadvantage of on-policy rollouts relative to teacher forcing. Read left to right, the top row of Figure 1 shows how the two bottlenecks accumulate. Moving from digits L8 to base36 L32 raises target difficulty and stalls both reverse-KL variants, while both forward-KL variants still reach the teacher ceiling. At essentially the same difficulty ( 185 185 versus 184 184 nats), lengthening the code from 23 23 to 64 64 tokens then collapses on-policy forward KL while PD remains strong, isolating rollout coverage. At document-specific positions where the student assigns little probability to teacher-preferred tokens, the objective should shift toward forward KL to restore the missing gradient, while the rollout should shift toward the teacher to keep later target positions reachable. Applying these interventions everywhere, however, would discard OPD’s main advantage: training on the student-generated states encountered at inference. We therefore propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), which intervenes only where teacher and student disagree and otherwise reduces to OPD. The gate opens on document-specific content that the student does not yet cover and closes once the student covers it. 7 Conclusion We analyzed why on-policy distillation becomes inefficient for knowledge injection, identifying weak reverse-KL supervision and limited student-rollout coverage. Based on this analysis, we proposed APD, which selectively adapts both the loss and rollout where teacher–student divergence is large. Our experiments show that the two failures are addressed in order, since sampling from the teacher helps only once the loss can raise the low token probabilities of the student, and that intervening at a small set of high-divergence positions already removes most of the deficit of OPD. Limitations We study knowledge injection, where the teacher holds information that the student cannot infer, so their distributions differ sharply on the content to be injected. We therefore do not test general distillation, where the student already produces a distribution close to that of the teacher, and other bottlenecks may dominate there. Our experiments cover two 8B backbones and two document-QA benchmarks, so how the two bottlenecks change with model scale and domain remains open. Most real-data evaluation questions and references are model-generated. Open-book checks and the smaller human-written question sets support their validity, but generator artifacts may still affect absolute scores or method rankings. Our comparisons measure learning efficiency at fixed budgets—400 steps in the testbed and 10 epochs on real documents—rather than asymptotic injection capacity, and additional compute or method-specific tuning could alter the ordering. The controlled key–code testbed deliberately removes linguistic structure and uses one training configuration, so it isolates the two mechanisms but does not establish how frequently they dominate natural knowledge injection. Finally, APD has similar FLOPs and wall-clock time to OPD when memory is sufficient, but because the teacher must stay resident during generation, it cannot offload one model while the other runs, which may limit scaling to larger models or longer contexts. Appendix B Datasets All documents, questions, and answers used in our experiments are in English. B.1 Benchmarks and Metrics We use QASPER and BioASQ because they provide long, knowledge-intensive documents in specialized fields (science and medicine), human-written question–answer pairs that can serve as demonstrations for generating evaluation questions, and established metrics. QASPER. QASPER contains information-seeking questions about NLP papers. Each document is a full paper of up to approximately 9 9 k tokens and fits within our 16,384 16{,}384 -token context window. Answer-F1 is token overlap between the generated and gold answer after standard normalization, maximized over gold references. We also report precision and recall because closed-book answers vary in length: recall tracks whether the injected content surfaces, while precision tracks whether it is stated without padding. We score only answerable questions because success on an unanswerable question measures abstention rather than retention of document content. BioASQ. BioASQ contains biomedical factoid questions, each paired with the full text of the PMC article that answers it. The model returns up to five ranked candidates: strict accuracy requires the top candidate to exactly match the gold answer or a listed synonym, lenient accuracy accepts a match anywhere in the list, and MRR uses the rank of the first correct candidate. B.2 Data Generation Each dataset contributes twenty test single-document units, QASPER papers and PMC articles paired with BioASQ factoid questions, and BioASQ also contributes ten development units for selecting τ \tau (Appendix C.3 ). A unit corresponds to one training run and contributes one observation to the paired tests reported throughout. Every unit carries three question sets: the benchmark’s human-written questions (two to six per QASPER paper, 72 72 in total over the test units of which 62 62 are answerable; one per BioASQ article, 20 20 in total), a training set, and a generated evaluation set. C.4 Baseline Settings Every baseline uses the method-specific hyperparameters of its original paper, whereas the training setup shared by all methods (optimizer, learning rate, number of epochs, batch size, and maximum length; Appendix C.2 ) is ours. In their original papers, most on-policy baselines first fine-tune the student with SFT and then distill into it. We instead distill into the student without this step, to measure injection under the largest information asymmetry between student and teacher. Appendix E.5 shows that APD remains the best method when every method is first fine-tuned with SFT. Below we describe the baselines whose settings need comment. GKD. We run GKD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) with a student-data fraction of λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , which the authors call mixed sampling, and the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence with β = 0.5 \beta=0.5 . The original work treats both as task-dependent hyperparameters and tunes them per task. We did not repeat that search for every setting, but our ablation on Llama-3.1 and BioASQ (Table 2 ) covers part of it, varying the sampling source and the direction of the KL divergence, though not the Jensen–Shannon divergence. MiniLLM. We follow the official implementation of MiniLLM ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , including teacher-mixed sampling with α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 , single-step regularization, and length normalization, with two differences. We omit the auxiliary language-modeling loss on a pretraining corpus, which our setting does not have. We perform one policy update per rollout instead of four, as for the other on-policy methods.
